The other thing we have run across is on units that go unoccupied and have negative building pressures, the fans can spin backwards. When the building goes occupied if the fan ramp up times are fast nuisance alarms can be created. If both of these have been checked it is possible, but unlikely that the VFD's are not sensing the correct voltage. If this is an intermittent problem to prove or disprove that the incoming voltage is the issue and that the drive is not the problem a three phase voltage data recorder can be used to see if voltage spikes are happening.If we need to get a tech out to assist further please don't hesitate to bring Dawn in the loop.

Variable Refrigerant Flow System SDM-21: Unoccupied Setpoints Current Condition: The commands for the VRF system are setup so that a heating and cooling setpoint is scheduled through the building automation system, however the local thermostats can only take a command of one setpoint. The system currently operates by averaging the heating/cooling BMS setpoints and sending the average setpoint to the thermostats. Since the heating and cooling setpoints are generally close to each other, for example 70F/72F, the system can maintain comfortability during occupied hours because it would send a 71F setpoint command. For a typical VRF system, the facility would want to set unoccupied heating and cooling setpoints so that nighttime system operation is minimal. Typically, those setpoints would be 60F for heating and 85F for cooling. However, due to the nature of this system, the 60F heating setpoint and the 85F cooling setpoint are averaged and local thermostats respond to a 72.5F setpoint. This is leading the units to operate at night and on the weekends. During the heating season, the average setpoint is causing the units to operate more during periods when the facility is unoccupied than when it is occupied. Recommendation: The RCx team recommends that controls team adjust the programming so that the system is able to send actual unoccupied setpoints, which will enable the system to de-energize during unoccupied periods.

Tug and secure the wires around the cone of the fan to avoid damages to the wires and plugs.- Loosen all the fan bolts, start removing them from the bottom, The fans are resting on a ledge which keeps the bottom part secured. For large fans it’s recommended to use two people for that task. - After the fans are removed from the wall the wiring and flex conduit between the quick connect box (the small box on the bulkhead) and the main controls box needs to be removed. It was explained that these overrides were put in place because when the pumps were originally scheduled to shut off at night, the condensers would still operate and damage the heat exchangers. Carrier informed us that they previously checked into this issue and found that the flow switches, which prevent the condenser units from operating when there is no condenser water flow, had been “jumped out”. Carrier claims that this has been resolved and that the flow switches should be operational. The RCx team was unable to test the operation of the flow switches due to the communication for the VRF system being down during testing. Additionally, due to how the unoccupied setpoints are currently programmed for the VRF system, the water-cooled condenser units operate more than necessary during unoccupied hours. Based on the email from Bruce Beddow it looks like the manufacturer recommends keeping these valves open at all times due to how slowly they open. Recommendation: The RCx team recommends that Carrier verify and provide a written statement that all flow switches are operational during their next preventative maintenance site visit. If all programming is in place then the RCx team recommends closing the valves and hence the pumps off when there is no call for heating and or cooling during unoccupied hours. The new system operation should then be fully commissioned to verify intended operation.

The sequence calls for the units to be programmed with dehumidification and economizer modes, however these modes are not currently programmed. Also, the supply air temperature should be reset based on outside air temperature; however during testing the units operated off a manual setpoint. If the return air humidity level rises above the humidity setpoint, the unit should go into dehumidification mode. In this mode, the DX cooling energizes to maintain a 55°F leaving cooling temperature and the hot gas reheat valve modulates to reheat the air to the 70°F supply air James Polk Elementary School – Retrocommissioning Report temperature setpoint (adjustable). Once the return air humidity level drops below setpoint, the unit will resume normal operation. If the outside air conditions are favorable and the unit is requesting cooling, the economizer mode should be energized. During this mode, the mechanical cooling will be de-energized and the enthalpy wheel shall control the supply air temperature setpoint. Recommendation: The RCx team recommends that the facility team and RCx team discuss the original design intent for the ERUs, the current facility requirements, and what programming changes are necessary to bring the units back to the required operation parameters.

The compressor must be set to disable during heating mode, and the heat will be controlled by an external coil in the duct. The coil will be controlled entirely by Siemens controls so the DOAS 2 unit needs only to go into fan only operation during heating mode.

Kurt was tracing voltage to the indoor BS boxes and reported that he wasn’t get any. Went to the master outdoor unit which was outputting 16VDC but, was not getting any voltage downstairs and the system was not initializing after a hard reset. Found that the communication wire going inside was broken inside of the liquid tite. The liquid tite connections for high and low voltage terminate into the bottom of the outdoor units which allow for water to enter when raining or during defrost. When the water freezes, ice forms inside of the liquid tite and disturbs the wiring. JCM sealed the connections with silicon in Friday but, water was already in the connections from being in service for months. Ran a temporary wire from 4C Master to the dog house junction box and spliced into the existing wire. Pulled in the correct count and the system started and ran. A new communication wire needs to be ran, would recommend somehow draining water out of all liquid tite if possible. ***Kurt noticed that multiple BS boxes only had 120V to them. The electricians during startup were supposed to fix this issue when it was found on all apts. ***Sealing off electrical connections was noted during startup. Went back down to the ITM to check on System 4C which was now pulled in but, systems 2A, 7A & 8A were now in a communication alarm. These three systems are on the same port. Went to the roof and disconnected the ITM chain, Systems 2A & 8A started but, systems 7A did not. Found that the controls contractors had used wire nuts in a junction box by the piping doghouse. Water had gotten in the wire nut connections which was distributing communications. Redid the connections and the system started, hooked back up the ITM daisy chain and all systems are online again. ***A new control wire should be pulled without splices going to system 7A. ***Noted during startup that splices in communication wiring is not recommended. Please use the following URL to view related photos/videos:https://vision.xoeye.io/partners/havtech/activity/C69A3910-5AF9-40E8-AF35-00A219BC443D

One is a low suction pressure alarm, two would be a high head pressure alarm, Three would be a PTS or PTD sensor alarm. The PTS sensor alarm means the suction pressure transducer isn’t functional and the Microtech III see a value of -43psi, which would cause the compressor not to run when commanded to. PTD alarm is the unit isn’t seeing a reading from the discharge pressure transducer.  We didn’t have a traditional low pressure switch to simulate low pressure within the circuit. Really the only way to make the compressor go into alarm manually was to pull one of the two transducers or the high pressure switch. We chose to pull the suction transducer. The controls tech confirmed the alarm down at the front end, and we plugged the transducer back in. - Dirty filter alarm - we pulled the 24VAC off the transducer and it went into dirty filter alarm. Also covered the low side of the transducer with my thumb which simulated a clogged filter. We went through all of these on both units.
